title: Simulated hackathon judging of Join
brief:
Act as a panel of three judges for the PayPal AI Hackathon on Devpost (judges are PayPal developer advocates and engineers). Score the submission "Join" strictly and honestly. Don't be generous.

Material, read-only:
- Code: D:\paypal\join (the repository; public at https://github.com/gino6178/join). Read README.md, docs/devpost.md, docs/demo-video-script.md, api/src/** (especially pay/, negotiate/, mcp.js, ops.js), web/src/**, examples/**.
- Official rules: D:\paypal\pdf\Devpost-Official-Rules.pdf, and a summary of the rules in D:\paypal\research\devpost-sources.md.
- Do not edit any files.

Facts about the build that you can't see from the code:
- Everything has been run end to end on the real PayPal sandbox: Orders v2 AUTHORIZE, partial final capture, void, refund, Payouts and Vault setup tokens all succeeded. Payer approval in that run used PayPal's published sandbox test card instead of a buyer login.
- 22 automated tests pass, including an end-to-end run of four agents over MCP.
- The demo video doesn't exist yet; the script is in docs/demo-video-script.md.
- Assume the video will be made as scripted.

Judging criteria (equally weighted, Rules §6): Technological Implementation, Design, Potential Impact, Innovation/Idea, Presentation. Stage One is pass/fail on fitting the theme and applying the required APIs/SDKs.

Deliver, in English:
1. Stage One: pass or fail, with the reason.
2. A table: each criterion scored 1-10 by each of the three judges (give each judge a distinct lens: a PayPal API engineer, a product/design lead, a developer advocate focused on AI/agents), plus the average, with 2-3 concrete justifications per criterion that point to files.
3. Likely prize outcomes: chances for Grand, each Honorable Mention (Most Creative, Most Impactful, Best Demo Delivery, Best Use of PayPal + AI, Best Use of Agentic Commerce), and Bryntum / APIMatic / Render sponsor prizes, as rough probabilities with reasons. Assume about 24,000 registrants and perhaps 800-1,500 real submissions.
4. **Technological Implementation deep dive:** list which PayPal products and APIs are used versus which a PayPal API engineer would expect or be impressed by. Rank the missing ones by score impact per day of work. Consider:
   - JS SDK v6 buttons, Venmo, Pay Later
   - Invoicing
   - Transaction Search / Reporting
   - Webhooks management API
   - Disputes
   - Subscriptions
   - PayPal Agent Toolkit or MCP used in code
   - Multiparty / platform fees
   - Fastlane
   - Package tracking
   - Anything else
   
   Be specific about how each would fit Join's flow, not generic.
5. The top 5 weaknesses a judge would write in their notes, each with a concrete fix.

Be concise but complete.

# Join: Devpost submission text

Draft for the Devpost form. Fill in the links marked TODO before submitting.

---

## Tagline

Your agent gets the group together, haggles with the venue and splits the bill with PayPal. You see every step.

## Inspiration

AI agents can already find a free time and a few friends. Then they stop: someone still has to call the venue, agree a
price, front the money and chase three people for their share. That last mile, the money, is where group plans die:
the badminton game, the karaoke night, the escape room, the barbecue.
And it's exactly the part nobody wants to hand to an agent without limits and a way to check what it did.

## What it does

Join is an agent-ready marketplace for getting a group together: sports courts, karaoke rooms, escape rooms, board
game tables, barbecue pits, dinner tables. It runs no AI model of its own. People bring their own agents
(Claude, or any MCP or A2A agent) and Join supplies the rules and the money:

- **Find a plan.** Who is free, and the fairest venue for each time: the one where the longest trip in the group is
  shortest.
- **Negotiate with the venue.** Each venue sets its own rules on Join: list price, off-peak, group and last-minute
  discounts, how far it will come down (firm, standard, eager) and a floor that is never revealed. Agents offer and
  counter; the venue's last counter is its best and final. The rules are enforced in code, so an agent can't probe for
  the floor or talk its way past it.
- **Over budget? Alternatives from the map.** When a price is over a person's limit, or the venue says no, the answer
  comes with other venues and free public places nearby, ranked by budget, time and trip, each with a reason.
- **Split it, negotiate it, pay it with PayPal.** The organizer guarantees the whole booking (an authorization, not a
  charge), so nobody can hold a room for free. The others are invited; their agents join or decline, and can ask to
  pay less, which the organizer's agent accepts or refuses. Each player pays their own share with PayPal, approved by
  them, or by their agent from saved PayPal within the limits they set. When everyone has paid, the booking is locked.
  The venue is paid afterwards.
- **See every step.** The website shows each person what the agents did, in words Join writes from the facts:
  every search, offer, counter-offer, invitation and payment.
- **Receipts anyone can check.** Every locked, refunded or paid-out booking gets a signed receipt: the negotiation,
  each payment and its PayPal ids, players only as hashes. It can be checked in the browser or with a script that
  shares no code with Join. (Optionally, batches of receipts can also be timestamped on a public chain.)
- **Limits only people can set.** Per-booking and per-week limits and allowed venues are set by the person on the
  website. Agent tokens can read them, never change them.

# Join, re-scored after the PayPal changes (same three judges)

**Verdict:** the gaps J1 and J3 flagged in round 1 are mostly closed, so the total goes from 32.0 to 34.0 out of 50. Join is still not a Grand Prize favourite: Impact and Presentation now hold it back. I read the latest commit and took your sandbox facts as given; I didn't run anything.

## 1. Scores

| Criterion | J1 PayPal eng. | J2 Product/design | J3 DevRel AI | Avg (was) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Technological Implementation | 8 | 8 | 7 | **7.7** (6.7) |
| Design | 7 | 6 | 7 | **6.7** (6.3) |
| Potential Impact | 5 | 6 | 6 | **5.7** (5.3) |
| Innovation/Idea | 7 | 7 | 8 | **7.3** (7.0) |
| Presentation | 6 | 6 | 7 | **6.3** (6.7) |
| **Total (of 50)** | 33 | 33 | 35 | **34.0** (32.0) |

**What raised scores:**
- **JS SDK v6.** Real buttons from a client token, a popup approval, and Pay Later and Venmo shown only when PayPal says the payer is eligible (`D:\paypal\join\web\src\components\PayPalButtons.jsx`, `paypal.js` `clientToken`).
- **Agent Toolkit in real code.** `D:\paypal\join\api\src\pay\toolkit.js` does reconciliation, invoices for extras and dispute listing. `D:\paypal\join\examples\venue-agent.mjs` loads the toolkit as an in-process MCP server.
- **More PayPal surface:**
  - Invoicing v2 for paying the organizer back, with Payouts sending them the money.
  - `provide-evidence` with the signed receipt. This also lifts Innovation, because it gives the receipt a PayPal use.
  - The Webhooks management API (`ensureWebhook`, 14 events).
  - The refund-webhook and `game_status` bugs are fixed.
- **The README now explains** why Join uses Payouts instead of multiparty.

**What still costs points, and the new problems:**
- **The money for extras never reaches the venue (J1).** `billExtras` invoices from Join's own account. `checkBills` marks the invoice paid, but nothing pays it out, so Join keeps the venue's $18.
- **"The venue's PayPal account" is really Join's.** `venue-agent.mjs` and `toolkit.js` both use Join's app credentials from `api/.env`. So the venue's reconciliation and disputes run on the platform's account. That fits the Payouts model, but the comments say otherwise.
- **The toolkit on the server is called by code, not by AI (J3).** The one place an AI drives it, `venue-agent.mjs`, has never been run.
- **Paying the organizer back can invoice someone who never agreed (J2).** `requestReimbursement` only excludes people who declined or paid. So an invitee who never answered gets invoiced, which breaks the product's own rule, "nothing is started for anyone who hasn't said yes."
- **The docs claim more than ran (this is why Presentation went down).** devpost.md says "PayPal, all run on the sandbox", and the README says "Everything below has been run against the PayPal sandbox". Neither is true of:
  - `provide-evidence`
  - Pay Later or Venmo buttons (ineligible in your desktop sandbox)
  - the venue agent

  A PayPal engineer who tests one of these and finds it hasn't run will discount everything else.
- **Still missing:** the video, a hosted URL, Render, and multiparty (now explained, not built). The README still says "since 1 October" against a git log that is entirely 30 Oct.

## 2. Updated prize probabilities

| Prize | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Grand (any of 3) | 2–4% | 4–6% |
| Best Use of Agentic Commerce | 7–10% | 9–12% |
| Best Use of PayPal + AI | 4–6% | 8–11% |
| Most Creative | 3–5% | 3–5% |
| Best Demo Delivery | 2–4% | 2–4% (depends on the video) |
| Most Impactful | 1–2% | 1–2% |
| Bryntum | 15–25% | 15–25% (unchanged) |
| APIMatic / Render | ~0% | ~0% (Render 15–25% if done; see item 3) |

**Chance of winning anything:** about 35–40% (was 25–35%).
